title: Stroke and TIA
summary: Focused history taking, examiner guidance and timed practice.

domains.descriptor: Introduces self and role, confirms name and DOB, asks who the relative is, gains consent
Opens with an open question, listens without interrupting, uses a prompt
Establishes the time early, from the witness
Signals the move to closed questions
Face, arm, leg, speech, vision, balance, headache, vomiting, seizure, chest pain, neck pain (8 or more = 3; 5 to 7 = 2; 3 to 4 = 1)
Anticoagulants and antiplatelets, bleeding, surgery, trauma, previous brain bleed (all = 2; some = 1)
Vascular risk factors, previous TIA or stroke, full drug list, allergies, family history
Accurate summary, checks it, states urgent CT and stroke team
Plain language, appropriate pace, acknowledges anxiety

aim.text: Assess focused, patient-centred history taking in a time-critical presentation of suspected stroke, including collateral history from a relative.

items: Open with an open question, then move to closed questions.
Establish the time last known well from a witness, early.
Cover stroke symptoms and consider mimics.
Screen for thrombolysis and thrombectomy safety (anticoagulants, bleeding, surgery, trauma).
Establish premorbid function, explore concerns, and summarise with a plan.

candidateInstructions.text: You are the emergency department doctor. Mr David Okafor, 66, has arrived in Resus by ambulance.
Paramedic handover: glucose 6.8 mmol/L, BP 168/94, HR 92 irregular, SpO2 97% on air, GCS 15.
Take a focused history from the patient and his wife. Do not examine. At the end, summarise and state your initial plan.

actorBriefs.title: Actor brief: patient, Mr David Okafor

blocks.text: Manner: calm but frightened, mildly slurred speech.

Only after an open question: "I was having breakfast and my mouth felt strange. I dropped my cup, then my left arm went heavy. My speech feels funny too." After "anything else?": "My vision is a bit blurry on the left."

head: Topic
Response
rows: Left face droop, left arm heavy, left leg a little weak, slurred speech, left blurred vision
Headache, vomiting, double vision, dizziness, seizure, blackout, chest pain, palpitations, neck pain or injury
Hypertension, type 2 diabetes. One fainting episode last year, "nothing found"
Aspirin 75 mg, metformin, amlodipine, atorvastatin. No anticoagulants. No allergies
No surgery, trauma, bleeding, black stools or dental work in 3 months. No brain bleed or aneurysm
Ex-smoker (10 years), a few beers at weekends. Lives with wife, drives, gardens, fully independent
"I think it's a stroke like my dad." "Will I get my arm back? I don't want to be a burden."

actorBriefs.title: Actor brief: wife, Mrs Grace Okafor

items: Anxious, speaks quickly, stays close to her husband.
He was completely well at 08:30 at breakfast. His face drooped about ten minutes later. She rang 999 at 08:50.
His speech is "a bit worse" since.
Mentions last year's fainting episode only if asked about past history.
If not reassured: "Is he going to die?"

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr Shah, one of the emergency doctors. Can you tell me your full name and date of birth?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: David Okafor, 4th March 1960.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Thank you, David. And you are?

lines.speaker: Wife
lines.text: Grace, his wife.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: I'd like to ask about this morning, and then we'll move quickly with tests. Is that alright with you both?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Yes, of course.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Could you tell me what has been happening this morning, in your own words?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: I was having breakfast and my mouth felt strange. I dropped my cup, and then my left arm went heavy. My speech feels funny too.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Thank you. Take your time. Is there anything else you've noticed?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: My vision is a bit blurry on the left side. That's all.

modelInteraction.title: Collateral history and time last known well

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Grace, were you with David when this started? When was he last completely well, with no symptoms at all?

lines.speaker: Wife
lines.text: He was normal at 08:30. About ten minutes later his face drooped. I rang 999 at 08:50.
Last known well: 08:30. This is the key time for treatment decisions.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: That's very helpful. Has anything got better or worse since?

lines.speaker: Wife
lines.text: His speech is a little worse, I think.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: I'm going to ask some specific questions now, so short answers are fine. Any headache?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: No.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Any vomiting, double vision, dizziness or problems with balance?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: No double vision. No dizziness.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Any fit, blackout, chest pain or palpitations?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: No.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Any neck pain, or a recent neck injury or fall?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: No.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Have you ever had anything like this before, even a short episode that passed?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Never.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Which medicines do you take?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Aspirin 75, metformin, amlodipine and a statin.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Any other blood thinners, such as warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban or edoxaban? Any allergies?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: No blood thinners, only the aspirin. No allergies.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: In the last three months, any surgery, injuries, falls, bleeding, black stools or dental extractions?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: None.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Have you ever had bleeding in the brain, or been told you have an aneurysm?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: No.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Do you have any medical conditions? Any heart problems, such as an irregular heartbeat?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: High blood pressure and diabetes. Nothing with my heart that I know of.

lines.speaker: Wife
lines.text: He fainted last year. The hospital checked him but found nothing.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Thank you, Grace, that's useful. Does anyone in the family have strokes or heart disease? Do you smoke or drink?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: My father had a stroke at 70. I stopped smoking ten years ago, and I have a few beers at weekends.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Before this morning, what could you do for yourself day to day? Who is at home with you?

lines.speaker: Wife
lines.text: Everything. He drives, does the gardening, looks after himself completely.

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Just Grace and me at home.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: David, what do you think might be happening? What is worrying you most?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: I think it might be a stroke, like my dad. Will I get my arm back? I don't want to be a burden.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: I understand. Grace, is there anything you are worried about?

lines.speaker: Wife
lines.text: Is he going to die?

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: I understand why you're frightened. David is stable at the moment, and we are acting quickly, which gives him the best chance. I'll keep you both updated at every step.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Let me summarise, and please correct me. David, you've had sudden left-sided weakness, slurred speech and blurry vision on the left, starting about 08:40. You were last completely well at 08:30. You take aspirin but no other blood thinners, you have high blood pressure and diabetes, and you were fully independent before today. Is that right?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Yes.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: This could be a problem with the blood supply to part of the brain, so I'm arranging an urgent CT scan of your head, a heart tracing and blood tests, and the stroke team is being alerted so they can see you straight away. Do you have any questions?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: No. Thank you, doctor.

head: Task
Expected in this station
rows: Introduce yourself, check name and date of birth, gain consent, start with an open question, listen without interrupting, signpost, summarise, state a plan.

Last well 08:30. Left face droop, left arm and leg weakness, slurred speech, blurred left vision. High blood pressure, diabetes, possible irregular heartbeat (fainting last year). Aspirin only, no blood thinners. Fully independent before.

Collateral from the wife. Headache, vomiting, fit, blackout, chest pain, neck pain. Previous episodes. Bleeding or surgery in 3 months. Allergies, family history, smoking, alcohol, daily function, worries.
Say aloud: check glucose, ABCDE, urgent CT head with CT angiogram, ECG, bloods with clotting, IV access, alert the stroke team, monitor, nothing to eat or drink until a swallow check.
Acknowledge fear, stay calm, correct mistakes openly, say "I would ask the stroke consultant" when unsure, restate the time if anything changes.

head: Situation
Good response
rows: Recheck ABCDE and glucose, tell the stroke team now, note the time.
Protect the airway, call for help, follow the seizure protocol, repeat glucose.
Pause, acknowledge, offer a seat and a nurse, then carry on.
Use the wife and short yes or no questions.
Go straight to the safety screen and summary.
Say what you know, name the limit, and say you would ask a senior.

head: Medical term
Say instead
rows: A problem with the blood supply to part of the brain
A blockage in a blood vessel
A mini-stroke, a short warning episode
One side of the face drooping
A quick scan that takes pictures of the brain
A clot-busting drug through a drip
Removing the clot through a thin tube in an artery
Nothing to eat or drink for now
Something else that can look like a stroke

plainLanguage.text: Useful phrases: "last seen completely well", "any weakness or numbness?", "any trouble speaking or understanding?", "any blood thinners?"

head: Question
Model reply
rows: "It looks likely from what you describe. The scan will confirm it and show us the best treatment."
Will I get my arm back?
"I can't promise. The sooner we treat this, the better the chance of recovery, and we are moving as fast as we can."
"He is stable at the moment and we are acting quickly. I'll keep you updated at every step."
"High blood pressure, diabetes and an irregular heartbeat can all cause it. Tests will tell us more."
"A small number of people get bleeding in the brain. Without treatment the outlook is usually worse. The stroke team will go through it with you."
Why can't he eat or drink?
"Swallowing can be affected, and food could go down the wrong way. We'll check it first."
"Not for now. The stroke team will advise when it is safe, and there are driving rules we'll go through."
"Yes, for now. A nurse will look after you and update you."

patientQuestions.text: Tips: acknowledge the feeling first, use short sentences, check understanding, never over-promise, avoid false reassurance.

items: ABCDE, oxygen only if hypoxic.
Capillary glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia.
FAST and NIHSS, then alert the stroke team.
Urgent non-contrast CT head; CT angiography if thrombectomy is considered.
12-lead ECG for atrial fibrillation; bloods including clotting and group and save; IV access.
Monitor BP, heart rate, saturations and temperature.

examinerQuestions.question: What time windows apply to reperfusion?

items: Thrombolysis (alteplase or tenecteplase per local protocol): within 4.5 hours of onset, once haemorrhage is excluded.
Thrombectomy for a large vessel occlusion: generally within 6 hours; selected patients up to 24 hours from last known well, guided by advanced imaging.
Use the last known well time, not the time symptoms were noticed.
BP below 185/110 before thrombolysis and below 180/105 after.
Intracranial haemorrhage on CT, previous brain bleed, suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Recent major surgery or trauma, active internal bleeding, coagulopathy.
Therapeutic anticoagulation (recent DOAC, raised INR on warfarin).
Uncontrolled hypertension, glucose outside the safe range, recent stroke or head injury.
Others per local protocol.
Hypoglycaemia (check glucose first), seizure with Todd's paresis, migraine with aura.
Sepsis or delirium, syncope, Bell's palsy, functional neurological disorder.
Old stroke deficits worsening during infection.

examinerQuestions.question: A TIA with fully resolved symptoms: management?

items: Aspirin 300 mg immediately once haemorrhage is not suspected.
Specialist assessment within 24 hours.
ECG, bloods, glucose, brain and vascular imaging as indicated.
Secondary prevention (statin, BP control, smoking cessation, antithrombotic therapy) and driving advice.
What are your immediate actions and investigations?
What time windows apply to reperfusion treatment?
What are the contraindications and cautions for thrombolysis?
What are the common stroke mimics?
How would you manage a TIA with fully resolved symptoms?

examinerQuestionPrompts.text: Model answers are in Learning mode.

items: Say your priority first: "My immediate priority is..."
Use a structure (ABCDE, then investigations, then treatment).
Give times and numbers: 4.5 hours for thrombolysis, last known well, BP under 185/110.
Link the answer back to this patient.
If unsure, say what you know and that you would ask the stroke consultant.
Keep to the time; stop when the examiner moves on.
No last known well time.
Giving thrombolysis before a CT.
Skipping glucose or the blood thinner question.
False reassurance or firm promises.
Jargon without explanation, or interrupting the patient.
No summary or plan.
Clear pass: structured, time-critical, all key points.
Pass: most points, minor omissions.
Borderline: key omission (for example no last known well time) or poor communication.
Fail: disorganised, unsafe omissions or unprofessional.
Closed questions only.
Asking when symptoms were noticed, not when last well.
Forgetting anticoagulants and bleeding risk.
Not using the wife's collateral history.
Naming a firm diagnosis before assessment.
Time is brain. Last known well is the most important question.
Open first, then closed. The funnel captures the patient's story, then fills gaps safely.
Collateral history is essential when speech or comprehension is affected.
Check glucose in every suspected stroke.
Never skip the safety screen for anticoagulants and bleeding risk.
Premorbid function guides treatment decisions and prognosis.
Be honest about uncertainty when counselling an anxious patient and relative.
